question_details.title: At the end of 2025, will any of GiveWell's top charities perform mass deworming as their primary intervention?
question_details.description:
This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2020-08-04 23:00:00 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/4919). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

According to GiveWell's [Cost-Effectiveness Analysis](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1zLmPuddUmKsy3v55AfG_e1Quk-ngDdNzW-FDx0T-Y94) (CEA), mass deworming ranks among the very best global health interventions. The evidence for deworming comes primarily from a [single study](https://www.nber.org/papers/w21428), which showed large economic effects which were present a full decade after treatment. However, other studies have shown [little](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/langlo/article/PIIS2214-109X(16)30242-X/fulltext) to [no effect](https://www.cochrane.org/CD000371/INFECTN_deworming-school-children-low-and-middle-income-countries) of mass deworming on weight, cognitive ability, school attendance or other health outcomes, and the weight placed on the initial paper has proved [controversial](https://www.vox.com/2015/7/24/9031909/worm-wars-explained).

In GiveWell's CEA, deworming benefits are modeled as being entirely due to long-term economic effects like those seen in the study mentioned above. Despite being heavily discounted due to concerns about replicability, in expectation these economic effects are expected to dominate the short term health effects of the interventions.

Givewell's position is explained, in detail, in the following two blog posts:

- [Why I mostly believe in Worms](https://blog.givewell.org/2016/12/06/why-i-mostly-believe-in-worms/)

- [How thin the reed](https://blog.givewell.org/2017/01/04/how-thin-the-reed-generalizing-from-worms-at-work/)

Some more information is available in [this](https://www.givewell.org/international/technical/programs/deworming) evidence overview, written by GiveWell, which cites several papers, and [this](https://www.evidenceaction.org/a-summary-of-the-deworming-evidence-base/) evidence overview, which was written by Evidence Action. While Evidence Action does currently run a deworming programme, they have proved [capable](https://www.vox.com/future-perfect/2019/6/7/18654620/evidence-action-no-lean-season-givewell) of changing their minds on programmes when the evidence changes.

Currently, GiveWell lists seven [top charities](), of which four are deworming programmes.

question_details.resolution_criteria:
**At the end of 2025, will any of GiveWell's top charities perform mass deworming as their primary intervention?**

- Resolution will be according to the GiveWell [website](https://www.givewell.org/) on 2026/01/01.

- If GiveWell no longer maintains a list of "top charities", but allows donors to donate funds which will be re-granted at GiveWell's discretion, this question resolves positively if at least 10% of these regrants go to deworming charities in the year 2025.

- "Mass deworming" is taken to mean treating all or almost all of the individuals in a group for parasitic worms, without testing to see whether they have them. This is common practice due to the low cost and excellent safety profile of deworming medication, as well as the relative expense of testing.

- If a charity has multiple programmes, but GiveWell restricts its donations to a particular programme, that programme is considered to be the "primary intervention" for the purposes of resolution. Otherwise, whichever intervention the organisation spends most on is considered the "primary intervention".

- If deworming medication is administered in addition to something else, for example a vaccine or vitamin supplement, at the same time, then whether "deworming" is the primary intervention will be determined by whether the majority of the value of the programme comes from deworming, according to GiveWell's CEA.

- If GiveWell ceases to exist in a similar form, such that neither of the conditions for positive resolution above make sense, this question resolves ambiguously.

- Some of the text in this question has been adapted from [this](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/FAA22RbfgC68fRnRs/if-you-mostly-believe-in-worms-what-should-you-think-about) EA forum post, by the same author.

**Active remote monitoring of long-term conditions with mobile devices: a systematic review of cost-effectiveness analyses - npj Digital Medicine**
A systematic review of cost-effectiveness analyses (CEAs) published in npj Digital Medicine examined seven studies on mobile device-based active remote monitoring for long-term health conditions. Six of the seven studies found the interventions to be cost-effective, with four showing they were 'dominant'—improving health outcomes (measured in quality-adjusted life years) while reducing healthcare costs. However, significant uncertainty exists in the joint distribution of incremental costs and health outcomes, which may hinder widespread adoption by decision-makers. The review highlights methodological limitations, including underreporting of health economic analysis plans, distributional effects, and patient engagement impacts due to recent reporting standards. No study conducted subgroup analyses to assess how population heterogeneity influenced cost-effectiveness. Most studies used trial-based designs, with uncertainty possibly due to non-inferiority/feasibility trial designs, underpowered superiority trials, or disparities in digital literacy and adherence. Decision-analytic models were underused (only two studies), despite their ability to extrapolate outcomes over lifetime horizons and support early-stage product development. Costing methods varied widely—top-down costing yielded substantially lower estimates than bottom-up micro-costing—suggesting potential underestimation of system costs if key resources are omitted. The review also notes that external dashboards, while easier to set up, impose workflow burdens on healthcare staff, and full integration with electronic health records requires significant infrastructure investment. Future research should prioritize decision-analytic modeling, explore non-randomized quasi-experimental designs, and investigate optimal monitoring frequencies. Additionally, broader perspectives beyond healthcare systems—such as patient time costs and travel savings—should be incorporated. The findings support the potential of mobile-based remote monitoring but caution that current evidence is insufficient to justify broad adoption due to persistent uncertainty. Developers and analysts are urged to improve transparency in upfront cost reporting and deepen exploration of uncertainty drivers to strengthen value propositions.

**Loneliness interventions can be effective but do not yet offer a complete solution**
Research published by the American Psychological Association on October 23, 2025, indicates that interventions to reduce loneliness are effective but do not yet offer a complete solution to a growing global public health issue. Loneliness is linked to depression, anxiety, cardiovascular disease, and early mortality. According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, social disconnection is as harmful to health as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day. A meta-analysis of 280 studies involving over 30,000 participants found that all five major intervention types—social support, social network creation, social and emotional skills training, psychological interventions (like cognitive behavioral therapy), and psychoeducation—reduced loneliness, with psychological interventions showing the strongest effects. In-person programs were more effective than digital-only ones, and benefits lasted up to six months across children, adolescents, adults, and older adults. Mathias Lasgaard, PhD, lead author from the Central Denmark Region and University of Southern Denmark, explained that cognitive behavioral therapy helps individuals reframe negative social thoughts, reducing avoidance and improving relationships. The study, the most comprehensive in over a decade, highlights the need for scalable, evidence-based solutions. However, the certainty of the evidence was rated as 'low to very low' due to methodological flaws in many studies, including small sample sizes, high dropout rates, and inadequate recruitment of lonely individuals. Researchers recommend more rigorous, population-specific evaluations. Despite limitations, the consistent results across hundreds of studies strongly suggest that loneliness can be reduced through targeted interventions, guiding policymakers and practitioners while underscoring the need for future refinement.

**Estimating the effect on obesity of delaying tax-based interventions in Mexico: A modeling study**
A modeling study published on October 23, 2025, by PLOS examined the human costs of delaying the implementation of a policy to double the sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) and non-essential dietary fat (NEDF) taxes in Mexico. The study found that while all intervention scenarios—implemented in 2025, 2030, or 2035—resulted in similar obesity prevalence by 2040 (approximately 41.6%), earlier implementation yielded significantly greater health benefits. Implementing the tax in 2025 led to 74% more years lived without obesity and 54% more deaths averted compared to 2030, and 459% more years lived without obesity and 339% more deaths averted compared to 2035. The analysis underscores that the timing of policy implementation is critical: even if long-term outcomes converge, earlier action reduces disease burden and mortality. The study highlights that Mexico, which declared an epidemiological emergency for obesity and diabetes in 2016, has delayed implementing SSB tax increases since at least 2018, with no change as of February 2025. The findings emphasize the importance of quantifying the 'cost-of-delay' in public health, particularly for population-level interventions. The model accounts for historical trends in total energy intake (TEI), showing that early interventions face steeper energy intake trends, making their immediate impact appear less effective in short-term comparisons. However, over time, earlier interventions produce far greater cumulative benefits. The study also notes limitations, including reliance on meta-analytic mortality hazard ratios, assumptions about energy intake trends, conservative price elasticity estimates, and a closed cohort model that excludes future generations. Despite these, the results consistently support the urgency of timely implementation of evidence-based fiscal policies to combat obesity and related chronic diseases. The authors advocate for incorporating temporal dimensions into future public health modeling to better assess the real-world impact of policy delays.

By May 2025, the PHC administered 32 IPT doses and distributed 47 LLINs. Malaria testing and treatment capacity surged, with 48 children and 14 adults tested in March 2025 alone. Community trust was restored, with outreach sessions drawing over 80 attendees—far exceeding expectations. Residents like Blessing Osawe, Ivie Osaigbovo, and Eghosa reported improved health outcomes, with mothers now seeking care proactively. The PHC now serves 16,263 people across farming communities. The transformation exemplifies how targeted investment and community partnership can restore healthcare access in underserved regions, turning a neglected facility into a beacon of hope. **Acupuncture Under the Microscope: What Really Happens in the Body When Needles Are Inserted**
Acupuncture, a practice originating in ancient China, is based on the belief that health depends on the free flow of 'qi' energy through body meridians, with disruptions causing illness and needle insertion restoring balance. Modern medicine does not recognize qi but investigates physiological mechanisms that may explain pain relief in some patients. Neurophysiologists, such as Dr. Li Wei from the University of Hong Kong, suggest acupuncture triggers the release of natural analgesics like adenosine and endogenous opioids, contributing to its pain-relieving effects. The placebo effect also plays a significant role, with rituals, atmosphere, and expectations amplifying brain response; a meta-analysis from the Chinese University of Hong Kong found sham acupuncture (insertion into random points) produced comparable results, confirming psychological influence. Evidence is strongest for pain management: a Cochrane review of nearly 5,000 participants showed 10 sessions reduced migraine frequency from 6 to 3–4 days per month. The UK’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends acupuncture for preventing chronic headaches and migraines. The American College of Physicians acknowledges it as part of non-pharmacological treatment, with 33 studies confirming pain reduction, though it does not outperform physical therapy. The British NICE considers it a possible option for primary chronic pain, though effects typically last no longer than three months. A 2012 meta-analysis found slight joint pain reduction, and the American College of Rheumatology permits its use as an adjunct if tolerated. However, UK experts note minimal clinical benefit and high costs, deeming it economically unjustifiable. Some patients use acupuncture for severe conditions like dementia, stroke, or infertility, but evidence does not support efficacy. A 2020 Cochrane review found no cognitive improvement in dementia patients, with studies suffering from weak methodology and small samples. A systematic analysis of 33 studies concluded acupuncture did not improve neurological outcomes, with positive results attributed to bias and placebo effects. Acupuncture during embryo transfer does not increase pregnancy or live birth rates, according to a Cochrane review of dozens of studies—safe but clinically ineffective. The World Health Organization has established international standards to minimize risks, though serious complications are rare.
